metadata.title: Are Students Ready for a Technology-Rich World? What PISA Studies Tell Us

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The report uses PISA 2003 microdata for 15-year-olds (target population defined by age, not grade) and combines information from student questionnaires, school questionnaires, and an optional ICT questionnaire administered in a subset of countries. The analysis is presented as cross-country comparisons and OECD averages computed as simple arithmetic means across participating OECD countries (each country contributes with equal weight), which is a reporting convention rather than a student-level weighting variable. The excerpt does not specify the exact PISA sampling weights (e.g., student design weights) or replicate-weight procedures, so the weighting approach at the student level cannot be confirmed from the provided text. For analysts using the PISA database, the appropriate complex survey design weights and replicate methods should be applied to obtain correct standard errors and significance tests, consistent with PISA technical documentation.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This publication is a descriptive policy report based on PISA 2003 questionnaire indices and cross-tabulated comparisons of ICT access/use with mathematics performance, rather than an empirical machine-learning study that explicitly models cognitive outcomes using plausible values. Plausible values handling is therefore not applicable to the extraction schema for PV-based achievement modeling. Missing-data handling is not reported at the level of an explicit imputation/deletion rule for the analytic models; instead, the report provides general symbols for missingness in tables (e.g., not applicable, too few observations, withdrawn, not available).

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: PISA 2003 target population consists of 15-year-olds aged 15 years 3 months to 16 years 2 months at the beginning of the assessment period, enrolled in an educational institution regardless of grade or institution type and regardless of full-time/part-time status. All students completed the main PISA background questionnaire; the ICT questionnaire was administered only in the subset of countries shown in bold in the report’s map (32 countries took up the option in PISA 2003). The report also notes that table cells may be missing due to not applicable categories, too few observations (<30 students per cell), or technical withdrawal of data.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD report synthesizes evidence from PISA 2003 to describe students’ access to and use of ICT and to examine associations with mathematics performance. PISA 2003 assessed 15-year-olds in 41 countries (including all 30 OECD members) using mathematics as the main performance domain, with mathematics test booklets administered for 120 minutes per student across combinations totaling 390 minutes overall. ICT information comes from (i) student background questionnaires (35 minutes) and (ii) an optional 5-minute ICT questionnaire administered in 32 countries, plus a school questionnaire completed by principals. The report documents cross-country patterns in computer access (home vs school), frequency and type of ICT use (Internet/entertainment vs programs/software), attitudes, and confidence in performing routine, Internet, and high-level computer tasks. It emphasizes that observed relationships with performance do not establish causation and highlights equity concerns, especially for students lacking home computer access and for those with low confidence in routine/Internet ICT tasks.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction targets an official assessment framework, user guide, or technical manual without an empirical ML study. Sample sizes, ML algorithms, and predictive findings are intentionally null or empty per schema rules for non-empirical IEA/OECD documentation.
